stimuli.description: Black and white film depicting work accidents with simulated blood and mutilation ('It Didn't Have to Happen') as a stressor.
Color/sound videotapes of six different everyday outdoor settings: two natural (vegetation, water) and four urban (heavy traffic, light traffic, many pedestrians, few pedestrians).

tables.description: Describes the visual content and sound levels (dB) for the six recovery environments (Nature Vegetation, Nature Water, Urban Heavy traffic, Urban Light traffic, Urban Many pedestrians, Urban Few pedestrians).

Mean changes in ZIPERS factor scores (Fear, Anger/Aggression, Positive Affects, Sadness, Attentiveness/Interest) from pre-stressor baseline to post-recovery for Nature, Pedestrian mall, and Traffic environments, along with F-values and p-values for environmental differences.

limitations: Results cannot be generalized directly to longer term nature exposures involving active participation (e.g., wilderness back-packing).
Further studies needed to investigate psychophysiological influences across varied situations (e.g., unstressed, bored, or chronically understimulated individuals).
Research should examine person-based variables (e.g., perceived control) influencing recovery in natural/urban settings.
Heart monitoring methods used did not allow precise disentanglement of parasympathetic and sympathetic influences.
No objective procedures available for measuring information rate over time for non-static, audiovisual environmental displays.
